title: My day: what comes before, what comes after

summary.text: You can look out of the window and tell that it is morning. Can you look out and tell that it is Tuesday? You will put your own day in order with cards, and test which things can swap places. You will learn the four parts of a day, the words before and after, and the seven days of the week. You will also find out which parts of time come from the Sun, and which names people chose.
summary.art: A girl kneeling on the floor laying eight small paper cards in a row, with a window behind her showing a low morning Sun over coconut trees.

intro.hook: Three skies from one day are mixed up. Which one comes first after you wake up: A, B or C?
intro.text: C comes first. The Sun comes up in the morning. Then comes A, when the Sun is high. Then comes B, when it is dark and the stars are out. So the order is C, A, B. What comes after B? C comes again, because the next morning comes. A day has an order, and the order goes round and round. In this lesson you will put your own day in order.
intro.art: Three small square pictures side by side: a high Sun, a night sky with a Moon, and a Sun just rising over rooftops.

outcomes: I can tell morning, afternoon, evening and night apart, and say one thing I do in each.
I can put the things I do in a day in order, using first, next, then and last.
I can say what comes before and what comes after something in my day.
I can say the seven days of the week in order, and the day before and after any day.
I can use yesterday, today and tomorrow correctly.
I can say which parts of time come from the Sun, and which names people chose.

terms.meaning: The bright time when the Sun is up. A day can also mean one whole day and night together.
terms.example: We played all day. There are seven days in a week.

terms.meaning: The part that starts in the middle of the day, around lunch time. The Sun is high and it is hot.

terms.meaning: The part of the day when the Sun goes down and the light fades.

terms.meaning: The dark part, after the Sun has gone down and before it comes up again.

explanations.concept: The four parts of a day
explanations.context: This card names the four parts of a day. You sorted your day cards into these four parts.
explanations.definition: A day has four parts. They always come in the same order: morning, afternoon, evening, night.
explanations.description: Morning starts when the Sun comes up. Afternoon starts in the middle of the day, around lunch time, when the Sun is high. Evening is when the Sun goes down. Night is the dark part. After night, morning comes again. Here is a worked example. Kavya eats lunch, and the Sun is high. So it is afternoon. Which part comes next? Evening comes next. Now you try: you are in bed and the stars are out. Which part is it, and which part comes next? The four parts are not the same length. Night is the longest part. You sleep through most of it. People also do not all agree on where one part stops. Is 4 o'clock afternoon or evening? Families say it differently.
examples: Morning: the Sun is low, crows call, and you brush your teeth.
Afternoon: the Sun is high, your shadow is short, and you eat lunch.
Evening: the sky turns orange and lamps are lit.
Night: it is dark, the stars are out, and you sleep.
explanations.art: A circle cut into four parts labelled morning, afternoon, evening and night, with a small Sun or Moon in each part and an arrow going round.

explanations.context: This card explains the words before and after. You used them when you read your day cards in a row.
explanations.definition: Before means earlier. After means later.
explanations.description: Put three things in a row: brush your teeth, eat breakfast, wash your plate. Here is a worked example. Look at 'eat breakfast' in the middle. What comes before it? Brush your teeth. What comes after it? Wash your plate. Now look again. Eating breakfast is after brushing. It is also before washing the plate. So one thing can be before and after at the same time. It depends on what you compare it with. Now you try: what do you do just before you sleep? What do you do just after you wake up?
examples: You put on socks before shoes.
You dry yourself after a bath.
Lunch is after breakfast and before dinner.
explanations.art: Three cards in a row with arrows: a toothbrush, a plate of idlis and a plate being washed, with 'before' written under the first and 'after' under the last.

explanations.context: This card shows how to tell the order of things with four small words. You found in the Day Cards Test that some orders can change and some cannot.
explanations.definition: Putting things in order means saying what happens first, what happens next, and what happens last.
explanations.description: Here is a worked example. Meenakshi gets ready for a bath. First she fills the bucket. Next she pours water. Then she rubs soap. Last she dries herself. Some orders cannot change. You cannot dry yourself before you pour the water. You cannot brush your teeth before you wake up. Other orders are chosen by people. Some families bathe before breakfast. Some bathe after breakfast. Both days work. Now you try: tell how you eat a banana, with first, next and last.
examples: First peel the banana. Next eat it. Last put the peel in the bin.
First cut the lemon. Next squeeze it. You cannot squeeze first.
Bath then breakfast, or breakfast then bath. Both work.
explanations.art: Four small pictures in a row labelled first, next, then, last: a bucket filling, water poured from a mug, soap, a towel.

explanations.concept: The seven days of the week
explanations.context: This card gives the seven days of the week in order. You walked round them on the Week Ring.
explanations.definition: A week is seven days in a row. Each day has a name, and the names always come in the same order.
explanations.description: The days are Sunday, Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday and Saturday. After Saturday, Sunday comes again. So the week goes round like a ring. Here is a worked example. Today is Thursday. Which day comes after it? Say the days in order: Wednesday, Thursday, Friday. Friday comes after Thursday. Which day comes before it? Wednesday. Now you try: which day comes after Saturday? In Tamil the days are named after the Sun, the Moon and five planets. Sunday is Nyayiru, which means the Sun. Monday is Thingal, which means the Moon. Many calendars in India start the week on Sunday. In some countries the calendar starts the week on Monday. Both have the same seven days in the same order.
examples: After Monday comes Tuesday.
Before Sunday comes Saturday.
Seven days after a Friday, it is Friday again.
explanations.art: Seven cards in a ring on the floor, each with a day name, and an arrow going round from Saturday back to Sunday.

explanations.context: This card explains three words that move along with you: yesterday, today and tomorrow.
explanations.definition: Today is the day you are in. Yesterday is the day before today. Tomorrow is the day after today.
explanations.description: Yesterday is one sleep back. Tomorrow is one sleep ahead. Here is a worked example. Today is Wednesday. Yesterday is the day before, so yesterday was Tuesday. Tomorrow is the day after, so tomorrow will be Thursday. Now you try: today is Saturday. What was yesterday? What will tomorrow be? These three words move. When you wake up tomorrow, you will call that day today. The day you are in now will be called yesterday.
examples: Today is Monday. Yesterday was Sunday. Tomorrow is Tuesday.
The dosa you ate one sleep ago was yesterday's dosa.
Your birthday is tomorrow. That means one more sleep.
explanations.art: Three boxes in a row labelled yesterday, today and tomorrow, with a child standing on the middle box and a small bed drawn between each pair of boxes.

chart.title: One sleep back, one sleep ahead

explanations.context: This card explains what makes morning, afternoon, evening and night happen, again and again.
explanations.definition: The Earth is a big ball that turns round. It turns once in one whole day and night.
explanations.description: The Sun shines all the time. It lights up one half of the Earth. The other half is dark. The Earth turns, and you turn with it. When your place turns towards the Sun, it is morning for you. When your place faces the Sun fully, it is the middle of the day. When your place turns away, it is evening, and then night. So the Sun does not go anywhere at night. Your side of the Earth has turned away from it. This also means that it is not morning everywhere at once. When children in Chennai eat breakfast at 8 in the morning, children in Mexico are getting ready for bed.
examples: Hold a ball near a lamp. One half is lit and one half is dark.
Turn the ball slowly. A dot on it goes into the light and out again.
You can call a cousin far away and ask: is it day or night where you are?
explanations.art: A ball held next to a table lamp in a dark room, half lit and half dark, with a small sticker on the lit side.

chart.title: The Earth: one half lit, one half dark

explanations.context: This card asks where the week comes from. The Sun gives us day and night. It does not give us Monday.
explanations.definition: A week is a number of days that people agreed to count together. Today almost everyone counts in sevens.
explanations.description: A day comes from the Earth turning. Nobody chose that. A week is different. Nothing in the sky goes round in exactly seven days. People chose seven a very long time ago, and nobody is sure why. Other people chose other numbers. Long ago in the city of Rome, the market came every 8 days. In France, in the year 1793, the rulers made a week of 10 days. People there had to work nine days before a rest day. After some years France went back to seven days. People also chose where a day starts. Clocks and phones start a new day in the middle of the night. In the Indian calendar called the panchangam, the day starts at sunrise. In the Jewish and Islamic calendars, the day starts in the evening.
examples: A week of 7 days: Sunday to Saturday.
A market week of 8 days in old Rome.
A week of 10 days in France, from 1793.
explanations.art: Three paper strips one under the other, cut into 7, 8 and 10 boxes, each with a small label: our week, old Rome, France 1793.

explanations.context: This card shows that people are not the only ones who know the time of day. Bees, roosters and trees know it too.
explanations.definition: Many living beings keep the time of day inside their bodies, without any clock.
explanations.description: A honeybee remembers the time of day when she found food. In 1929 a scientist, Ingeborg Beling, put out sugar water at the same time each day. The bees learnt the time. The next day they came at that time, even when the dish was empty. A rooster crows before the Sun comes up. In 2013 scientists in Japan kept roosters in dim light all day and night. The roosters still crowed about once a day, at their own morning. A tamarind tree folds their small leaves at night and opens them in the day. The four o'clock flower opens late in the afternoon. All of them keep the parts of the day. As far as anyone knows, none of them keeps a week of seven days.
examples: Crows in a town fly to their sleeping trees before dark.
A hibiscus flower opens in the morning and closes by evening.
A touch-me-not plant folds their leaves at night.

perspectives.explanation: They call this a body clock. They describe it as chemicals inside each cell that rise and fall once a day.
The bee knows what time it is and chooses when to fly. Both ways describe the same thing that bees do.

explanations.art: A honeybee at a small dish, a rooster crowing in the dark and a tamarind branch with folded leaves, each with a small Sun or Moon beside them.

agreed.text: The Earth turns round once in a day. That is why morning comes, then night, then morning again.
agreed.evidence: In 1851 Léon Foucault hung a heavy ball on a long wire in Paris. As it swung, the line of its swing slowly turned over the floor. The floor was turning with the Earth.

agreed.text: It is not morning everywhere at once. When it is morning in India, it is night on the other side of the Earth.
agreed.evidence: You can test it with a phone call to someone far away. When it is 8 in the morning in Chennai, it is 8:30 at night in Mexico City.

agreed.text: The Sun does not make a week. People chose to count days in sevens.
agreed.evidence: Nothing in the sky goes round in exactly seven days. People have also used weeks of 8 days and 10 days.

agreed.text: Bees know the time of day without a clock.
agreed.evidence: In 1929 Ingeborg Beling fed bees at the same time each day. The next day the bees came at that time, even though the dish was empty.

challenging.claim: The Sun goes round the Earth once every day.
challenging.who: Almost everyone, for thousands of years
challenging.context: This card is about an old idea of why day and night happen.
challenging.for: It looks that way. The Sun comes up on one side, crosses the sky and goes down on the other side. Nobody notices the Earth moving.
challenging.against: Aryabhata wrote in the year 499 that the Earth turns. In 1851 Foucault's swinging ball showed the ground turning under it.

challenging.claim: The week has seven days because of the Moon.
challenging.context: This card is about why a week has seven days. Nobody is sure of the answer.
challenging.for: The Moon takes about seven days to grow from a half Moon to a full Moon. People long ago watched the Moon closely.
challenging.against: It takes a little more than seven days, so a week does not stay in step with the Moon. And other peoples used 8 or 10 days.

challenging.claim: A new day starts at 12 o'clock at night, for everyone.
challenging.context: This card asks where one day stops and the next day starts.
challenging.for: Clocks and phones all over the world change the date at 12 o'clock at night. It helps that everyone uses the same rule.
challenging.against: It is a rule people agreed on. The panchangam starts the day at sunrise. The Jewish and Islamic calendars start it in the evening.

big_questions.q: Where does evening stop and night begin? Can you point to the exact moment?
big_questions.hint: Watch the sky get dark one evening. Does it happen in one jump, or slowly?

big_questions.q: Breakfast is after brushing and before lunch. Can one thing be before and after at once?
big_questions.hint: Before what? After what? Try it with your day cards.

big_questions.q: Does a week have a first day? Or does it go round with no start?
big_questions.hint: Some calendars start on Sunday and some on Monday. Look at the Week Ring. Where does a ring begin?

big_questions.q: If everyone forgot the names of the days, would the days still come?
big_questions.hint: What would still happen every morning? What would be lost?

big_questions.q: A rooster crows before sunrise. Does he know it is morning? Does he know it is Sunday?
big_questions.hint: One of these comes from the Sun. One comes from people.

big_questions.q: It is morning for you and night for a child in Mexico. Whose time is the real one?
big_questions.hint: Each of you is looking out of your own window. Could both be right?

story.title: The Day Without a Name
story.note: Yazhini, Arul and Ammamma are made up. Weekly markets, called sandhai, that come on the same day every week are real in Tamil Nadu. So are wall calendars with one sheet to tear off for each day.
text: Yazhini was six, and it was the summer holidays. She was staying at Ammamma's house in a village near Thanjavur. Her cousin Arul was staying there too. He was eight.
Before she left, Amma had said, "I will come on Friday, by the morning bus."

At home, Yazhini always knew what day it was. Monday was the day of the drawing class. Saturday was the day Appa made dosas. But here, every day was the same. They woke up. They fed the hens. They climbed the guava tree. They slept. The days had lost their names.
One morning Yazhini woke up with a question. "Ammamma, is it Friday today?"
Ammamma was grinding batter. "I have lost count, kanna. Look at the calendar."
The calendar hung by the door. It was the kind with one small sheet for each day. But nobody had torn off a sheet since the holidays began. It still showed the day the children had come.
"Look at your phone," said Yazhini.
"The phone is at the repair shop," said Ammamma.
Arul laughed. "You don't need a phone. Just look outside. The sky will tell you."
So the two of them went out to the front step and looked.
The Sun was low, just above the coconut trees. The air was cool. The crows were making a great noise. A hen walked past with her chicks behind her.
"It is morning," said Yazhini.
"I know it is morning," said Arul. "Wait." He screwed up his eyes and looked at the sky for a long time. "It looks like a Thursday."
"What does a Thursday look like?"
Arul opened his mouth and shut it again. He could not say.
Yazhini looked up too. The sky was blue, the same as yesterday. The Sun was the same Sun. The crows did not look like Friday crows or Thursday crows. They only looked like crows.
"The sky does not say," she said slowly. "The sky only says morning."
"Then nobody knows," said Arul, and he went to look for a guava.
Yazhini sat down on the step. If the Sun did not tell her the name of the day, who could?
People could. People had names for days. So she had to think about people.

Then she remembered the sandhai. That was the market where they had bought the big jackfruit. Ammamma had said something then. "The sandhai comes only on Wednesday. If we miss it, we wait a whole week."
So the market day was a Wednesday. Yazhini was sure of that. She picked up a tamarind seed from the ground and put it on the step. "Wednesday," she said. "The market."
What came after the market? They came home. They ate jackfruit until their hands were sticky. They slept.
Then came the day it rained. She and Arul made paper boats and raced them in the drain. She put down a second seed, after the first. "Thursday. The boats."
What came after the boats? They slept again. And then she woke up with her question.
She put down a third seed. "Today."
She touched the seeds one by one. "Wednesday. Thursday." Her finger stopped on the third seed. "Friday. Today is Friday!"
Arul came back with a guava. "How do you know? Maybe there were two boat days."
"There was one boat day," said Yazhini. "It rained one time. One sleep before the boats, and one sleep after."
Arul looked at the three seeds. He counted the sleeps on his fingers. Then, far away on the main road, a bus horn sounded.
They ran. Ammamma came after them, wiping her hands. The morning bus stopped under the neem tree, and Amma stepped down with her blue bag.
That afternoon Arul stood in front of the calendar. "Show me how you did it," he said.

So Yazhini showed him. They tore off one sheet for each day that had gone, and said what they did on that day. The hen day. The guava day. The market. The boats. When they stopped, the sheet on top said Friday.
"And tomorrow?" asked Yazhini.
Arul thought. "Saturday."
"And yesterday was?"
"Thursday. The boats."
That evening the crows flew home over the coconut trees, the same as every evening. Yazhini watched them go. Nobody had told the crows that it was Friday. But Yazhini knew.
story.epiphany: For the parent: the sky can tell us the part of the day, but not the name of the day. The name comes from people. So Yazhini works it out from something people do on a fixed day, the Wednesday market. Then she counts the sleeps forward, one seed for each day. That is the unit's maths: order, before and after, and counting on along the week.
ask: Arul looked at the sky to find the day's name. Why did that not work?
What could Yazhini tell from the sky, and what could she not tell?
How do you find out the name of the day at your home?
If today is Friday, what day was two sleeps ago? How do you know?

experiments.title: The Day Cards Test: can the order of my day be changed?
experiments.context: In this test you draw eight things you do in a day on eight cards and put them in order. Then you swap two cards at a time. Before each swap you guess: will the day still work? You will find out which orders can change and which cannot.
experiments.question: If we swap two things in our day, does the day still work?
experiments.predict: Before each swap, guess: will the day still work, or will it go wrong? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We swap only two cards at a time, and they must be next to each other. After each swap we put the two cards back, so every swap starts from the same day.
results_table: My guess: works or goes wrong

materials.item: a sheet of paper cut into 8 cards
a pencil and crayons
a second sheet of paper, for the table and the four boxes

schedule.what: Draw eight day cards, put them in order, test five swaps, then sort the cards into the four parts of the day.

experiments.record: A grown-up draws the table. For each swap, write the two cards, the guess and what you found. At the end, the child says what they found, and the grown-up writes it under the table.

example_chart.title: What a finished table can look like (your cards and guesses will be your own)

setup.art: A sheet of paper cut into eight small cards on a floor, each with a simple child's drawing: a bed, a toothbrush, a bucket, a plate of idlis, a plate of rice, a ball, a plate of dosa, a pillow.
setup.caption: 1. Draw eight things you do in a day, one on each card.

setup.art: The eight cards laid in one row from left to right, a child pointing at the first card.
setup.caption: 2. Put the cards in order, from waking up to sleeping.

setup.art: Two hands swapping the second and third cards in the row, with curved arrows showing the swap.
setup.caption: 3. Swap two cards that are next to each other. Does the day still work?

setup.art: A sheet of paper with four boxes labelled morning, afternoon, evening and night, with the eight cards sorted into the boxes.
setup.caption: 4. Sort the cards into the four parts of the day.

flow.do: 1. Cut a sheet of paper into 8 cards. 2. Ask your child to tell you eight things they did yesterday, from waking up to sleeping. 3. Write one or two words on each card. 4. Your child draws a small picture on each card.
flow.say: Tell me eight things you did yesterday. Start with waking up. End with going to sleep.
flow.kid: Think of yesterday. Say eight things you did. Draw one on each card.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Day Cards Test. You make eight cards, one for each thing you do in a day.
flow.parent: If your child is stuck, use these eight: wake up, brush teeth, bath, breakfast, lunch, play, dinner, sleep. Stick figures are fine. The drawing should take about half a minute for each card.

chart.title: Eight cards, one for each thing you do

flow.do: 1. Shuffle the cards. 2. Ask your child to lay them in a row from left to right, in the order of the day. 3. Your child reads the row aloud with first, next, then and last.
flow.say: These are all mixed up. Put them in the order you did them. Then read me your day.
flow.kid: The cards are mixed up. Lay them in a row, in order. Read your day aloud.
flow.context: This is step 2 of the Day Cards Test. You put your eight day cards in order, from waking up to sleeping.

ask.q: What did you do first? What did you do last?
What did you do just before lunch? What did you do just after lunch?
good: Before lunch I had a bath.

flow.parent: Do not correct the order yet. If two cards are in an order you did not expect, ask about them in the next step.

flow.do: 1. Draw the table. 2. Point at the first two cards. 3. Ask for a guess and a reason, and write the guess. 4. Swap the two cards. 5. Your child acts out the new order, or tells it. 6. Write what you found. 7. Put the cards back.
flow.say: I will swap these two cards. Will your day still work, or will it go wrong? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at your first two cards. Guess: can they swap? Now swap them and act it out.
flow.context: This is step 3 of the Day Cards Test. You swap the first two cards in your day, and see whether the day still works.

ask.q: What happened when you tried the new order?
good: I cannot brush my teeth when I am asleep.

flow.parent: With 'wake up' and 'brush teeth', the swap goes wrong: nobody brushes while asleep. Accept any guess that comes with a reason. Let the acting out give the answer.

flow.do: 1. Test four more swaps the same way. 2. You choose two pairs. Your child chooses two pairs. 3. Each time: guess and reason, swap, act it out, write, put back. 4. Try bath with breakfast. Try dinner with sleep.
flow.say: Now you choose two cards that are next to each other. Guess first. Will the day still work? Why?
flow.kid: Choose two cards next to each other. Guess first. Then swap them and see.
flow.context: This is step 4 of the Day Cards Test. You test four more swaps, and guess before each one.

ask.q: Which swaps went wrong? Which swaps still worked?
good: Wake up has to be first.

flow.parent: Bath and breakfast can swap, and many families do it each way. Dinner and sleep cannot. Your child may say that a swap 'works' when you expected 'goes wrong'. Ask them to act it out. Their reason matters more than the answer.

flow.do: 1. Draw four boxes on the second sheet. Write morning, afternoon, evening, night. 2. Your child puts each card in its box. 3. Count the cards in each box together.
flow.say: A day has four parts. Which part does each card belong to? How do you know?
flow.kid: Here are four boxes for the four parts of the day. Put each card in its box.
flow.context: This is step 5 of the Day Cards Test. You sort your eight day cards into morning, afternoon, evening and night.

ask.q: How did you know that card belongs to the morning?
good: The Sun has just come up.
I do it after I wake up.

ask.q: Which part of your day has the most cards?

flow.parent: Morning usually has the most cards, because getting ready takes many small steps. If a card could go in two boxes, let your child choose and say why.

check.q: You eat lunch and the Sun is high in the sky. Which part of the day is it?
check.why: It is afternoon. Afternoon starts around lunch time, when the Sun is high. Picking morning usually means thinking of any bright time as morning.

chart.title: Four parts, always in this order

flow.do: 1. Lay the eight cards in a ring, in order. 2. Ask what comes after the sleep card. 3. Look at the table together. 4. Ask your child what they think, what they saw and why. 5. Write their words under the table.
flow.say: Look at our table. Which swaps went wrong? Which worked? What is different about them?
flow.kid: Put your cards in a ring. What comes after sleep? Now look at your table. Which swaps worked?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Day Cards Test. You say what you found: which orders in a day can change and which cannot.

ask.q: What do you think now? What did you see? Why is it so?
good: Wake up has to come before everything.
Bath and breakfast can swap, because we choose that.
After sleep, I wake up again.

flow.parent: A strong answer has two kinds of order in it. One kind cannot change. The other kind is chosen by the family. Read the card 'First, next, then, last' after this step, not before.

check.q: Which two things can swap places, and the day still works?
options: Dinner and sleeping for the night
check.why: Bath and breakfast can swap. Some families bathe first and some eat first. You cannot brush before you wake, and you cannot eat dinner after you are asleep.

chart.title: After sleep, wake up comes again

activities.title: The Window Test: what can the sky tell you?
activities.context: In this activity you look out of a window without looking at a clock or a calendar. You find out what the sky can tell you about time, and what it cannot tell you.
activities.problem: Can you tell the part of the day by looking outside? Can you tell the day of the week?

materials.item: a window or a balcony
paper and a pencil
a calendar or a phone, kept hidden until the end

activities.safety: Never look straight at the Sun. Look at where the light and the shadows fall.

schedule.what: Look outside, guess the part of the day and the day of the week, then check both.

activities.record: Draw two columns: 'The sky told me' and 'People told me'. Write or draw each clue in one column.

setup.art: A girl and her mother at an open window of a flat, looking out at rooftops, a low Sun and long shadows, with a wall clock behind them covered by a towel.
setup.caption: 1. Look outside. Do not look at a clock.

setup.art: The same window view with small circles drawn round four clues: the Sun, a long shadow, a crow and a milk seller on a cycle.
setup.caption: 2. Find clues. Which part of the day is it?

setup.art: A sheet of paper with two columns headed 'The sky told me' and 'People told me', with small drawings in each.
setup.caption: 3. Now guess the day of the week. Who can tell you?

flow.do: 1. Hide the clock and the phone. 2. Stand at the window with your child. 3. Ask which part of the day it is. 4. Ask for the clues.
flow.say: Do not look at a clock. Look outside. Is it morning, afternoon, evening or night? How can you tell?
flow.kid: Look out of the window. Which part of the day is it? Find three clues.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Window Test. You look outside and find clues that tell you the part of the day.

ask.q: What clues did you find?

flow.parent: Good clues are the height of the Sun, how bright it is, how long the shadows are, and what birds are doing. Remind your child not to look straight at the Sun.

flow.do: 1. Stay at the window. 2. Ask which day of the week it is. 3. Ask your child to find a clue outside. 4. Write down the guess.
flow.say: Keep looking outside. Which day of the week is it? What can you see that tells you?
flow.kid: Keep looking. Which day of the week is it? Can you see a clue outside?
flow.context: This is step 2 of the Window Test. You try to tell the day of the week just by looking outside.

ask.q: Does the Sun look different on a Sunday?
good: It looks the same every day.
I cannot tell from the Sun.

ask.q: Is there any clue at all?
good: The shop is shut, so maybe it is Sunday.
The school van came, so it is not Sunday.

flow.parent: The sky gives no clue at all. Your child may find clues from people: a shut shop, a school van, a weekly market. Notice together that every one of these clues comes from people.

chart.title: Seven days. Which one is today?

flow.do: 1. Show the calendar or phone and check the day. 2. Draw two columns on the paper. 3. Sort each clue: did the sky tell us, or did people tell us? 4. Ask who told us the name of the day.
flow.say: Let us check. Today is this day. Who told us the name of the day? The sky, or people?
flow.kid: Check the day on a calendar. Now sort your clues. Did the sky tell you, or did people?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Window Test. You sort your clues into what the sky told you and what people told you.

ask.q: What could the sky tell you? What could it not tell you?
good: It told me it is morning.
It could not tell me it is Tuesday.
Only the calendar knows the day.

flow.parent: This step is where the Roots card comes from. The part of the day comes from the Sun. The name of the day comes from people. Let your child say it in their own words.

check.q: Which of these can you find out just by looking at the sky?
check.why: You can see that it is morning, because the Sun is low and the light is new. The sky looks the same on every day of the week, so it cannot show Sunday or a birthday. People keep those names.

activities.title: The Week Ring: yesterday, today, tomorrow
activities.context: In this activity you lay the seven days of the week in a ring on the floor and walk round it. You find today, yesterday and tomorrow with your feet.
activities.problem: Which day comes after Saturday? And where do yesterday and tomorrow go when today moves?

materials.item: 7 sheets of paper or newspaper
a thick pencil or a crayon
a calendar or a phone, to check today's day

schedule.what: Lay the seven day sheets in a ring, find today, then hop to tomorrow, yesterday and further.

activities.record: Draw a ring of seven circles. Write the first letter of each day in the circles. Colour today.

setup.art: Seven sheets of paper in a ring on a floor, each with a day name written large, Sunday at the top and the days going round like a clock.
setup.caption: 1. Write one day on each sheet. Lay them in a ring, in order.

setup.art: A girl standing on the sheet marked Wednesday, pointing ahead to Thursday.
setup.caption: 2. Stand on today. One hop forward is tomorrow.

setup.art: The same girl hopping backward from Wednesday to Tuesday, with a small arrow.
setup.caption: 3. One hop back is yesterday.

flow.do: 1. Write one day name on each sheet, in big letters. 2. Say the seven days together, twice. 3. Your child lays the sheets in a ring, in order. 4. Saturday and Sunday end up next to each other.
flow.say: Let us say the days: Sunday, Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday. Now lay them in a ring, in that order.
flow.kid: Say the seven days. Lay the seven sheets in a ring, in order.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Week Ring. You lay the seven days of the week in a ring on the floor.
flow.parent: If your child does not read yet, draw a small Sun on Sunday and say each name as you lay the sheet. Saying the days in order is the first skill. Do not hurry it.

flow.do: 1. Check today's day on the calendar. 2. Your child stands on today. 3. Ask what tomorrow is. Your child hops one sheet forward and says the day. 4. Go back to today. Ask what yesterday was. Your child hops one sheet back.
flow.say: You are standing on today. Tomorrow is one sleep ahead. Hop to tomorrow. What day is it?
flow.kid: Stand on today. Hop one sheet forward. That is tomorrow. Say the day.
flow.context: This is step 2 of the Week Ring, seven day sheets in a ring on the floor. Here you find tomorrow and yesterday.

ask.q: What did we do yesterday? What will we do tomorrow?
good: Yesterday we went to the park.

flow.parent: Tie each hop to something real that happened yesterday or will happen tomorrow. That makes the words stick.

chart.title: One hop back, one hop forward

flow.do: 1. Call out a day. Your child jumps to it. 2. Ask for the day after it and the day before it. 3. Do this five times. 4. Make sure one of the days is Saturday.
flow.say: Jump to Saturday. Which day comes after Saturday? Hop and see.
flow.kid: Jump to the day you hear. Then hop to the day after it.
flow.context: This is step 3 of the Week Ring, seven day sheets in a ring on the floor. Here you find the day before and the day after any day.

ask.q: Is there a last day of the week?
good: After Saturday it is Sunday again.
Saturday is last on the calendar, but then it starts again.

flow.parent: Many children think nothing comes after Saturday, because the calendar row ends there. The ring shows that Sunday comes next.

check.q: Today is Saturday. What day is tomorrow?
options: There is no day after Saturday
check.why: Tomorrow is Sunday. The week goes round like a ring, so after Saturday comes Sunday again. Picking Friday means hopping back instead of forward.

flow.do: 1. Your child stands on today again. 2. Ask them to guess where seven hops forward will end. 3. They hop seven times, saying each day. 4. Ask what they notice.
flow.say: Stand on today. If you hop forward seven times, where will you land? Guess first, then try.
flow.kid: Stand on today. Guess where seven hops will take you. Now hop and count.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Week Ring, seven day sheets in a ring on the floor. Here you hop seven times and see where you land.

ask.q: Where did you land? Why?
good: There are seven days, so seven hops go all the way round.

flow.parent: Seven hops bring your child back to the same day. That is why next week's Monday is seven sleeps after this Monday.

activities.title: Maths in the kitchen: the lemon juice robot
activities.context: In this activity a grown-up is a robot who makes lemon juice. The robot does exactly what your six cards say, in the order you lay them. You find out why cooks must get the order right.
activities.problem: A recipe is a list of steps in order. What happens to the lemon juice if the order is wrong?

materials.item: a lemon
a tumbler of drinking water
sugar
salt
a spoon, a knife and a small plate
paper cut into 6 cards, and a pencil

activities.safety: Only a grown-up uses the knife.

schedule.what: Make six step cards, lay them in order, run the robot without food first, then make the lemon juice.

activities.record: Stick or copy the six cards in the final order on a sheet. Put a star on the steps that could swap.

setup.art: Six small paper cards on a kitchen counter with simple drawings: a knife and lemon, a squeezed lemon half, a tumbler of water, a spoon of sugar, a spoon stirring, a child drinking.
setup.caption: 1. Make six cards, one for each step.

setup.art: A child laying the six cards in a row on the counter while a mother stands stiffly with arms bent like a robot.
setup.caption: 2. Lay the cards in order. The robot does what they say.

setup.art: The mother stirring a tumbler of lemon juice while the child points at the fifth card.
setup.caption: 3. Run the robot. Fix the order if it goes wrong.

flow.do: 1. Write one step on each card: cut the lemon, squeeze the lemon, pour the water, add sugar and salt, stir, drink. 2. Your child draws a small picture on each. 3. Shuffle the cards.
flow.say: These six cards make lemon juice. But they are mixed up. I am a robot. I only do what the cards say.
flow.kid: Draw a picture on each card. These six steps make lemon juice.
flow.context: This is the first step of the lemon juice robot. You make six cards, one for each step of making lemon juice.

flow.do: 1. Your child lays the six cards in a row. 2. Do a pretend run with no food. Act out each card in order, like a robot. 3. If a step cannot be done, stop and say 'Robot stuck'. 4. Your child fixes the order.
flow.say: Lay the cards in the order I should do them. First we do a pretend run, with no lemon.
flow.kid: Lay the cards in a row. The robot will act them out. Fix the row if the robot gets stuck.
flow.context: This is step 2 of the lemon juice robot. A grown-up acts out your six cards in order, without food, to test the order.

ask.q: Why did the robot get stuck?
good: You cannot squeeze a lemon before it is cut.
You cannot stir when nothing is in the tumbler.

flow.parent: Play it straight. If 'squeeze' comes before 'cut', try to squeeze a whole lemon and fail. If 'drink' comes first, lift an empty tumbler. The pretend run wastes no food.

flow.do: 1. Now run it for real. 2. You cut the lemon. 3. Your child squeezes, pours, adds sugar and salt, and stirs, reading each card. 4. Your child tells the order with first, next, then and last.
flow.say: Now we make it for real. Read me the first card. What comes next?
flow.kid: Now make the juice. Read each card in order. A grown-up cuts the lemon.
flow.context: This is step 3 of the lemon juice robot. You make real lemon juice by following your six cards in order.
flow.parent: Let your child do every step except the cutting. Ask 'What comes next?' before each card.

flow.do: 1. Drink the juice together. 2. Point at the cards. 3. Ask which two cards could swap places and still give good juice. 4. Ask which could never swap.
flow.say: Which two cards could swap places, and the juice would be just as good? Which could never swap?
flow.kid: Drink your juice. Which two cards could swap? Which could never swap?
flow.context: This is the last step of the lemon juice robot. You find which steps of the recipe can swap places and which cannot.

ask.q: Why can water and sugar swap, but not cut and squeeze?
good: The lemon must be open before the juice comes out.
Stirring has to come after everything is in.

check.q: Which step must come before 'squeeze the lemon'?
check.why: You must cut the lemon first. A whole lemon gives almost no juice. Stirring and drinking come after the juice is in the tumbler.

activities.title: Which takes longer? Count the claps
activities.context: In this activity a grown-up claps slowly and counts while you do four small jobs. You find out which job takes the longest time, by counting.
activities.problem: Some things in your day are over quickly and some take long. How can you tell which takes longer without a clock?

materials.item: a pair of chappals, a towel and a tumbler of water
paper and a pencil

schedule.what: Guess which of four jobs takes longest, count claps for each job, then put the jobs in order.

activities.record: Write the four jobs and the number of claps for each. Then write them again in order, shortest first.

example_chart.title: One family's claps (yours will be different)

setup.art: A pair of chappals, a folded towel, a steel tumbler of water and a pencil and paper laid in a row on the floor.
setup.caption: 1. Get ready four jobs: chappals, towel, water, your name.

setup.art: A father clapping steadily with a speech bubble '1, 2, 3' while a girl slips on her chappals.
setup.caption: 2. A grown-up claps slowly and counts. You do the job.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with four rows: a drawing of each job and a number of claps beside it.
setup.caption: 3. Write the claps. Which job took longest?

flow.do: 1. Name the four jobs: put on both chappals, fold the towel, drink half the water, write your name. 2. Ask which will take longest and which will be quickest. 3. Write the guesses.
flow.say: Here are four jobs. Which one will take the longest? Which will be the quickest? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at the four jobs. Guess which takes longest. Guess which is quickest.
flow.context: This is the first step of Count the Claps. You guess which of four small jobs takes the longest time.

flow.do: 1. Say 'go'. Clap slowly and evenly, about one clap each second, and count aloud. 2. Stop when the job is done. 3. Write the number of claps. 4. Do all four jobs. Clap at the same speed each time.
flow.say: When I say go, start the job. I will clap and count until you finish.
flow.kid: Start when you hear 'go'. Do the job. Listen to the claps being counted.
flow.context: This is step 2 of Count the Claps. A grown-up claps slowly and counts while you do each of four small jobs.
flow.parent: The claps must be the same speed for every job, or the numbers cannot be compared. Clapping along with a ticking clock helps. Your child should not rush: this is not a race.

chart.title: Each dot is one clap (an example)

flow.do: 1. Read the four numbers together. 2. Your child puts the jobs in order, from fewest claps to most. 3. Compare with the guesses. 4. Ask why the claps had to be the same speed.
flow.say: Which job had the most claps? So which took the longest? Put them in order, shortest first.
flow.kid: Look at your four numbers. Which job took longest? Put the jobs in order.
flow.context: This is the last step of Count the Claps. You put four small jobs in order from the shortest time to the longest.

ask.q: What would go wrong if I clapped fast for one job and slowly for another?
good: The numbers would not be fair.
The fast one would get more claps.

check.q: Folding a towel took 14 claps. Putting on chappals took 6 claps. Which took longer?
check.why: Folding the towel took longer. More claps at the same speed means more time. 14 is more than 6.

activities.title: Everyone keeps time: a morning and evening watch
activities.context: In this activity you look outside twice in one day, once in the morning and once before dark. You find out what birds and plants do at each time.
activities.problem: People have clocks. How do crows and flowers show that they know the part of the day?

materials.item: a window, a balcony or a doorstep
paper and a pencil

activities.safety: Never look straight at the Sun.

schedule.what: Morning: watch for five minutes. Draw what the birds and plants are doing.
Evening, before dark: watch for five minutes from the same place. Draw what has changed.

activities.record: Fold a sheet in half. Draw the morning on one half and the evening on the other half.

setup.art: A girl at a balcony in the morning, with crows on a wire, an open hibiscus flower in a pot and sparrows on the railing.
setup.caption: 1. Morning: watch for five minutes. What are birds and plants doing?

setup.art: The same balcony in orange evening light, with crows flying in a line across the sky and the hibiscus flower closed.
setup.caption: 2. Evening: watch again from the same place. What has changed?

setup.art: A folded sheet of paper with a morning drawing on the left half and an evening drawing on the right half.
setup.caption: 3. Draw both. Who knew the time without a clock?

flow.do: 1. In the morning, stand at the window with your child for five minutes. 2. Look for birds, flowers and leaves. 3. Your child draws what each one is doing.
flow.say: What are the birds doing now? Are the flowers open or closed? Draw what you see.
flow.kid: Watch for five minutes. What are the birds doing? Are flowers open? Draw them.
flow.context: This is the first step of the morning and evening watch. In the morning you draw what birds and plants are doing.
flow.parent: Any living being will do: crows, pigeons, mynas, sparrows, a hibiscus or a tulsi in a pot, a tree across the road. If you have a tamarind or a touch-me-not nearby, look at their leaves.

flow.do: 1. Before dark, go back to the same place for five minutes. 2. Your child draws what has changed. 3. Ask who told the birds it was evening.
flow.say: Look at the same birds and plants. What is different now? Who told them it is evening?
flow.kid: Watch again. What has changed since morning? Draw it. Who told the birds it is evening?
flow.context: This is the last step of the morning and evening watch. Before dark, you see what the same birds and plants do now.

ask.q: Do the crows have a clock? How do they know when to fly home?

flow.parent: In many towns crows fly together to their sleeping trees before dark. A hibiscus flower that was open in the morning is often closed by evening.
flow.wait: Do this step in the evening of the same day

check.q: A hibiscus flower opens in the morning and closes by evening. What does this show?
options: The plant keeps the time of day
The plant has a clock on the wall
check.why: The plant keeps the time of day in their own way, with no clock. Many plants and animals do.

games.title: Fill My Day
games.players: 1 to 4 players: alone, with a parent or with friends
games.context: This is a card game with 16 cards. Each card shows something that happens in the morning, afternoon, evening or night. You collect one card for each part and lay them in order. It builds quick sorting into the four parts of the day.

printables.title: 16 day cards to cut out. The part of the day is on the back of each card

items.f: The Sun is high in the sky
The hottest time of the day

printables.title: A day mat: 4 boxes in a row (one mat for each player)

rules: Each player has a day mat with four boxes in a row: morning, afternoon, evening, night. To make one by hand, draw four boxes and write the four words.
Shuffle the 16 cards. Put them in a pile with the backs facing down, so nobody sees the answers.
On your turn, take the top card. Read it aloud, or ask a grown-up to read it. Say which part of the day it belongs to.
Turn the card over to check. If you are right and that box on your mat is empty, put the card in the box.
If that box is already full, or you named the wrong part, put the card at the bottom of the pile.
The first player to fill all four boxes says their day aloud: 'In the morning I… In the afternoon I…' and wins.
Playing alone: count how many turns you need to fill your mat. Play again and try to need fewer.

setup.art: A paper mat with four boxes in a row labelled morning, afternoon, evening and night, and a pile of small cards face down beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Each player takes a day mat. Put the cards in a pile, answers facing down.

setup.art: A child holding up a card that says 'Brush your teeth' and pointing at the morning box.
setup.caption: 2. Take a card. Say which part of the day it belongs to.

setup.art: A day mat with one card in each of the four boxes, and a child reading along the row with her finger.
setup.caption: 3. Fill all four boxes. Then say your day in order.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 16 cards, or write them on slips of paper. 2. Draw a day mat for each player. 3. Shuffle the cards. Put them in a pile with the answers facing down. 4. Read the rules aloud.
flow.say: Each card is something that happens in a day. You need one card for each part of the day.
flow.kid: Take a day mat. Put the cards in a pile, answers facing down.
flow.context: This is the first step of Fill My Day, a card game about the four parts of a day. Here you set up the mats and cards.

flow.do: 1. Play one practice turn each. 2. Take a card and read it. 3. Ask which part of the day it belongs to, and why. 4. Turn it over to check. 5. Place it or put it back.
flow.say: This card says 'Lamps and lights come on'. Which part of the day is that? How do you know?
flow.kid: Take a card. Say which part of the day it is. Say how you know.
flow.context: This is step 2 of Fill My Day, a card game about the four parts of a day. Here you practise naming the part for a card.

check.q: The card says 'The Sun comes up'. Which box does it go in?
check.why: It goes in the morning box. Morning starts when the Sun comes up. In the evening the Sun goes down.

flow.parent: Sunrise and sunset are the cards children mix up most. Ask: is the day starting or ending?

chart.title: Which box does your card go in?

flow.do: 1. Shuffle again and play the game. 2. Each player says the part of the day before placing a card. 3. Now and then, ask a player which parts they still need.
flow.say: You have morning and night. Which parts do you still need? Which of them comes first?
flow.kid: Play the game. Say the part of the day for every card you take.
flow.context: This is step 3 of Fill My Day, a card game about the four parts of a day. Here you play until someone fills their mat.

ask.q: You have morning and night. Which two parts are missing?

chart.title: Two boxes full, two to go

flow.do: 1. When someone fills all four boxes, they read their day aloud in order. 2. Every other player reads the cards they have, in order too.
flow.say: Your mat is full. Tell me your day, from morning to night.
flow.kid: Your mat is full. Say your day in order, from morning to night.
flow.context: This is the last step of Fill My Day, a card game about the four parts of a day. Here the winner reads their day in order.

games.title: Round the Week
games.players: 1 to 4 players: alone, with a parent or with friends
games.context: This is a dice game played on a ring of seven squares, one for each day of the week. You say the day you will land on before you move. Each time you get round to Sunday, you win a bean. It builds quick counting on through the days.

printables.title: 7 day squares to cut out and lay in a ring, in this order

rules: Lay the seven squares in a ring, in order. Each player puts a button on Sunday. Put a small heap of beans in the middle.
On your turn, roll the dice. Before you move, say the day you will land on. Count on through the days to find it.
Now move your button one square for each dot. If you land on the day you said, stay there. If not, go back to where your turn began.
Each time you land on Sunday or go past Sunday, take one bean. One bean means one whole week.
The first player to have 3 beans wins.
Playing alone: count how many rolls you need to win 3 beans. Play again and try to need fewer.

setup.art: Seven paper squares in a ring on a floor with the day names, a star on Sunday, two buttons on Sunday and a small heap of beans in the middle.
setup.caption: 1. Lay the seven days in a ring. Put your buttons on Sunday.

setup.art: A dice showing 3 beside a button on Friday, and a child with a speech bubble 'Saturday, Sunday, Monday'.
setup.caption: 2. Roll. Say the day you will land on. Then move.

setup.art: A button moving past the Sunday square and a hand taking one bean from the heap.
setup.caption: 3. Each time you reach or pass Sunday, take a bean.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the seven squares, or write the days on slips of paper. 2. Lay them in a ring, in order. 3. Give each player a button. 4. Read the rules aloud.
flow.say: This is a race round the week. Every time you come round to Sunday, you win a bean.
flow.kid: Lay the seven days in a ring. Put your button on Sunday.
flow.context: This is the first step of Round the Week, a dice game on a ring of the seven days. Here you set up the ring.

chart.title: The board: seven days in a ring

flow.do: 1. Play one practice turn each. 2. Show how to count on. 3. If you are on Friday and roll 3, touch the next three squares and say Saturday, Sunday, Monday.
flow.say: I am on Friday and I rolled 3. I count on: Saturday, Sunday, Monday. I will land on Monday.
flow.kid: Roll the dice. Count on through the days. Say where you will land.
flow.context: This is step 2 of Round the Week, a dice game on a ring of the seven days. Here you practise counting on through the days.

check.q: You are on Friday and you roll 3. Where do you land?
check.why: You count on Saturday, Sunday, Monday, and land on Monday. Landing on Sunday means Friday was counted as the first step.

flow.parent: Counting the square you are standing on as 'one' is the most common slip. The first step always lands on the next day.

flow.do: 1. Play the game. 2. Each player says the day before moving. 3. Give a bean each time a button reaches or passes Sunday. 4. Now and then, ask how many days are left until Sunday.
flow.say: You are on Thursday. How many more days until Sunday? What roll do you need?
flow.kid: Play the game. Say your day before you move. Take a bean at Sunday.
flow.context: This is step 3 of Round the Week, a dice game on a ring of the seven days. Here you play and win a bean for each week.

ask.q: You are on Thursday. How many days until Sunday?

chart.title: Sunday is day 1. The arrow is on Thursday.
chart.unit: the next Sunday comes after day 7

flow.do: 1. When someone has 3 beans, the game ends. 2. Ask each player which day they finished on. 3. Ask which roll would bring a player back to the same day.
flow.say: Who has three beans? Which day did you finish on? Could one roll of the dice ever bring you back to the same day?
flow.kid: The first to win 3 beans wins. Which day did you finish on?
flow.context: This is the last step of Round the Week, a dice game on a ring of the seven days. Here you finish the game.
flow.parent: No roll of one dice brings you back to the same day. That needs seven steps, and a dice stops at six.

projects.title: My Week Strip: seven days, one picture a day
projects.context: In this seven-day project you draw one small picture each evening of something that happened that day. At the end you have your whole week in a row, and you can say what happened before and after each day.
projects.problem: A day that is over is easy to forget. How can you keep a week so that you can look back at it in order?

materials.item: a long strip of paper, made by taping two sheets end to end
a pencil and crayons
a button or a coin, as the today marker

schedule.what: Draw seven boxes on the strip and write the days, starting from today. Draw one thing from today in the first box.
Move the marker to today. Say what you did yesterday. Draw one thing from today.
Move the marker. Say yesterday, today and tomorrow. Draw today's picture.
Move the marker. Count the days done and the days left. Draw today's picture.
Move the marker. Say what happened two days ago. Draw today's picture.
Move the marker. Guess what you will draw tomorrow. Draw today's picture.
Draw the last picture. Read the whole week aloud in order.

projects.record: The strip is the record. Keep it on the wall or the fridge for the week.

setup.art: A long strip of paper with seven empty boxes in a row, a day name written above each box, taped to a wall at a child's height.
setup.caption: 1. Draw seven boxes. Write the days above them, starting from today.

setup.art: A girl drawing a small picture of a kite in the third box, with a button stuck above that box as a marker.
setup.caption: 2. Each evening, move the marker to today and draw one thing.

setup.art: The finished strip with seven small drawings, and the girl pointing along it while her grandmother listens.
setup.caption: 3. On the last day, read your week aloud in order.

flow.do: 1. Tape two sheets end to end. 2. Draw seven boxes in a row. 3. Write today's day above the first box, and the next six days in order. 4. Your child draws one thing from today in the first box.
flow.say: This strip will hold one whole week. Today goes in the first box. What happened today that you want to keep?
flow.kid: Draw seven boxes in a row. Draw one thing from today in the first box.
flow.context: This is day 1 of My Week Strip, a seven-day project. You draw one small picture each evening, to keep your week in order.

chart.title: Day 1: one box done, six to go

flow.do: 1. Move the marker to the second box. 2. Point at the first box and ask what day that was, and what happened. 3. Your child draws one thing from today.
flow.say: The marker is on today. Look at the box before it. What do we call that day now?
flow.kid: Move the marker to today. What did you draw yesterday? Now draw today.
flow.context: This is day 2 of My Week Strip, a seven-day project. You draw one small picture each evening, to keep your week in order.

challenges.title: Stretch: what day will it be after 10 sleeps?
challenges.context: This is a puzzle that goes past Class 1. You find out what day it will be after 10 sleeps, and then after bigger numbers of sleeps. You invent a quick way that does not need you to hop every single day.
challenges.problem: Your cousin is coming to stay after 10 sleeps. What day of the week will that be? Find a way that also works for 15 sleeps and 21 sleeps.
constraints: You must check your answer in a second way.
Your way must work when you start from any day of the week.
You may use the Week Ring, beans, paper and a pencil.
materials: the seven day sheets from the Week Ring, or seven slips of paper
a calendar, to check at the end
challenges.safety: Keep seeds, beans and buttons away from babies and toddlers, who could choke on them.
general: Stand on today on the Week Ring. Hop forward 10 times and say each day.
Write the days in one long line and count along the line.
Put one bean on each day sheet, going round, until 10 beans are down.
creative: Seven sleeps always bring back the same day. So 10 sleeps is one whole week and 3 more sleeps. Hop only 3.
Put the beans in a row of 7 and a row of what is left. Only the short row matters.
Make a small table: after 7 sleeps, the same day. After 8, one day on. After 9, two days on.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own way. Use it for 15 sleeps and for 21 sleeps. Check each answer by hopping round the Week Ring.

setup.art: Seven day sheets in a ring on a floor with a child standing on Wednesday and ten beans in her hand.
setup.caption: 1. Stand on today. You have 10 sleeps to count.

setup.art: Ten beans laid out in two rows on the floor: a row of seven and a row of three.
setup.caption: 2. One way: lay 10 beans as a row of 7 and a row of 3.

setup.art: The child hopping three sheets forward from Wednesday to Saturday, with the row of three beans beside her.
setup.caption: 3. Seven sleeps bring the same day. Hop only the 3 that are left.

flow.do: 1. Lay the Week Ring. 2. Your child stands on today. 3. Ask what day it will be after 10 sleeps. 4. Let them find it in their own way. 5. Write the answer.
flow.say: Your cousin comes after 10 sleeps. What day will that be? Find out any way you like.
flow.kid: Stand on today. Find the day after 10 sleeps. Use any way you like.
flow.context: This is the first step of the 10 sleeps puzzle. You find the day after 10 sleeps in your own way.
flow.parent: Most children hop ten times round the ring. That is a good first way. Many lose count near seven or eight, which is why a second way is needed.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to hop exactly 7 times from today. 2. Ask where they landed. 3. Try 7 hops from two other days. 4. Ask what 7 hops always do.
flow.say: Hop seven times from today. Where do you land? Try from another day. What do you notice?
flow.kid: Hop 7 times from today. Where do you land? Try from another day.
flow.context: This is step 2 of the 10 sleeps puzzle. You find out what seven sleeps always do.

ask.q: What do seven hops always do?
good: They bring me back to the same day.
Seven sleeps is one whole week.

chart.title: Seven hops go all the way round

flow.do: 1. Lay 10 beans in a row. 2. Ask your child to push 7 of them together into one week. 3. Count the beans left over. 4. Your child hops only that many from today. 5. Compare with the first answer.
flow.say: Here are 10 sleeps. Push seven of them together. That is one week, and it brings the same day. How many sleeps are left?
flow.kid: Lay 10 beans. Push 7 together. Count what is left. Hop only that many.
flow.context: This is step 3 of the 10 sleeps puzzle. You split 10 sleeps into one whole week and the sleeps left over.

check.q: Today is Wednesday. What day is it after 10 sleeps?
check.why: Saturday. Seven sleeps bring Wednesday again. Three more sleeps are Thursday, Friday, Saturday. Picking Friday means Wednesday was counted as the first hop.

flow.parent: 10 is 7 and 3. Your child does not need to write this as a sum. Seeing the beans in a row of 7 and a row of 3 is enough.

chart.title: 10 sleeps: one week, and some more

flow.do: 1. Ask for the day after 15 sleeps. 2. Your child lays 15 beans and makes weeks of 7. 3. They hop what is left. 4. Try 21 sleeps. 5. Check one answer on a real calendar.
flow.say: Now try 15 sleeps. How many whole weeks can you make? How many sleeps are left over?
flow.kid: Now try 15 sleeps. Make rows of 7 beans. Hop what is left over.
flow.context: This is the last step of the 10 sleeps puzzle. You use your way for 15 sleeps and 21 sleeps.

ask.q: What happened with 21 sleeps?
good: It is the same day as today.

flow.parent: 15 beans make two rows of 7 and 1 left over, so the answer is one day on. 21 beans make three rows of 7 with none left, so it is the same day as today.

items.p: A day has 4 parts. The first part is shaded. Which part is it?
items.why: Morning is the first part of the day. It starts when the Sun comes up.

items.p: Put the four parts of a day in order. Start with morning.
items.why: The Sun comes up in the morning. It is high in the afternoon. It goes down in the evening. Then it is night.

items.p: Look at the row. 'Brush teeth' comes before 'eat breakfast'.
items.why: True. 'Brush teeth' is in box 1 and 'eat breakfast' is in box 2. Box 1 comes before box 2.

items.p: Count the boxes. How many days are in one week? ____
items.why: There are 7 boxes, one for each day: Sunday, Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday.

items.p: Which day comes just after Monday?
items.why: Say the days in order: Sunday, Monday, Tuesday. Tuesday comes just after Monday. Sunday comes before Monday.

items.p: Sunday is day 1 and Monday is day 2. Which day is the arrow on?
items.why: The arrow is on 4. Count the days: Sunday 1, Monday 2, Tuesday 3, Wednesday 4.

chart.title: The days of the week, numbered

items.p: Match each thing to its part of the day.
items.why: The Sun comes up in the morning and goes down in the evening. Lunch is in the afternoon. Stars show at night, when it is dark.

items.p: Yesterday is the day after today.
items.why: False. Yesterday is the day before today. It is over. The day after today is tomorrow.

items.p: Sort each thing: do you do it before you eat, or after you eat?
items.why: You wash your hands and serve the food first. You wash the plate and rinse your mouth when the eating is over.

items.p: Each dot is one sleep until Pongal. How many sleeps are there? ____
items.why: Count the dots: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. There are 5 sleeps until Pongal.

items.p: Draw one thing you do in the morning and one thing you do at night.
items.a: Two drawings that fit the two parts, such as brushing teeth for morning and sleeping for night.
items.why: A strong drawing shows something that really belongs to each part. A Sun or a Moon in the picture helps to show which part it is.

items.p: Say your answer aloud. A grown-up writes it. What did you do yesterday? Say three things in order.
items.a: Three things from yesterday, told in the order they happened, with words like first, next and last.
items.why: A strong answer keeps the real order and uses order words: first, next, then, last.

items.p: Draw the sky in the evening. Draw where the Sun is.
items.a: A Sun low in the sky, or half hidden, with orange or fading light.
items.why: In the evening the Sun goes down. A strong drawing puts the Sun low, not high.

items.p: A week has 7 days. The shaded days are over. How many days are left? ____
items.why: 2 boxes are shaded and 5 are not. 7 take away 2 leaves 5.

items.p: Today is Wednesday. What day was yesterday?
items.why: Yesterday is the day before today. The day before Wednesday is Tuesday. Thursday is tomorrow.

items.p: Today is Friday. What day is tomorrow?
items.why: Tomorrow is the day after today. The day after Friday is Saturday.

items.p: Put these in the order of a day. Start with waking up.
items.why: You wake up first. Breakfast is the morning meal, lunch is in the afternoon and dinner is at night. Sleep comes last.

items.p: After Saturday comes Sunday.
items.why: True. The week goes round like a ring. When Saturday is over, a new week starts with Sunday.

items.p: Today is Monday. Kavya's birthday is on Thursday. How many sleeps until her birthday? ____
items.why: Count on from Monday: Tuesday is 1, Wednesday is 2, Thursday is 3. So there are 3 sleeps.

chart.title: Sunday is day 1. The arrow is on Monday.

items.p: Sort each thing: does it come from the Sun, or did people choose it?
items.why: Morning, night and shadows happen because of the Sun, for everyone. The names of days, the seven-day week and holidays were chosen by people.

items.p: Match each day to the day after it.
items.why: Say the days in order and stop one day later. After Saturday the week starts again with Sunday.

items.p: Two cousins are getting ready in the morning.

views.says: Bath first, then breakfast. That is the right order.
Breakfast first, then bath. That is the right order.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Why? Then say one thing the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with a reason, then says the other order also works.
items.why: Both orders work. Bath and breakfast can swap places, and families choose. Some orders cannot swap, such as waking up and brushing.

items.p: Say your answer aloud. A grown-up writes it. In the Day Cards Test, which two cards could not swap? Why not?
items.a: Two cards such as 'wake up' and 'brush teeth', with a reason: you cannot brush your teeth while you are asleep.
items.why: A strong answer names two cards and gives the reason. One of them has to happen before the other can.

items.p: Draw the Week Ring. Colour today. Put a star on tomorrow.
items.a: Seven circles in a ring with the days in order, today coloured and a star on the next day round.
items.why: A strong drawing has seven days in the right order, and the star is one step forward from today.

items.p: Lessons on 5 days. Rest on 2 days. How many days in all? ____
items.why: 5 and 2 more make 7. That is one whole week.

items.p: Today is Sunday. What day is the day after tomorrow?
items.why: Tomorrow is Monday. The day after that is Tuesday. That is two hops forward from Sunday.

items.p: Today is Tuesday. After 7 sleeps it is Tuesday again. After 8 sleeps it is ____.
items.why: Seven sleeps bring the same day. One more sleep takes you one day on, to Wednesday.

items.p: The market comes every Wednesday. Today is Monday. How many sleeps until the market?
items.why: Count on from Monday: Tuesday is 1, Wednesday is 2. Picking 3 means Monday was counted as a sleep.

chart.title: Sunday is day 1. The arrow is on Monday.

items.p: Put these days in order. Start with Thursday.
items.why: After Thursday come Friday and Saturday. Then the week goes round to Sunday and Monday.

items.p: When it is morning in India, it is morning everywhere on Earth.
items.why: False. The Sun lights only half of the Earth at one time. When India has morning, the other side of the Earth has night.

chart.title: The Earth: one half lit, one half dark

items.p: Brushing took 9 claps. Folding took 14 claps. How many more claps did folding take? ____
items.why: Count on from 9 to 14: 10, 11, 12, 13, 14. That is 5 more claps.

items.p: The Sun looks different on Sundays.
items.why: False. The Sun looks the same on every day of the week. People gave Sunday its name.

items.p: The week began on Sunday. Today is Wednesday. Sort each day: over, or still to come?
items.why: The days before Wednesday are over: Sunday, Monday, Tuesday. The days after Wednesday are still to come: Thursday, Friday, Saturday.

items.p: Two calendars hang on a wall.

views.says: The week starts on Sunday. My calendar shows it.
The week starts on Monday. My calendar shows it.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Why? Then say what is the same in both calendars.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with a reason, then says both calendars have the same seven days in the same order.
items.why: Both are right. Where the week starts is a choice people made. The seven days and their order are the same in both.

items.p: A crow wakes at sunrise. Does the crow know it is Monday? Say why you think so.
items.a: Any answer with a reason. For example: the crow knows it is morning from the light, but Monday is a name people use.
items.why: A strong answer tells two things apart. The crow can see the part of the day. The name of the day is kept by people.

items.p: Draw a week with 5 days, not 7. Give each day a name of your own.
items.a: Five boxes in a row or a ring, each with a made-up name.
items.why: Any five names are right. People chose seven days and their names, so a different choice is possible.

items.p: Match each day to the day before it.
items.why: Say the days in order and stop one day earlier. Before Sunday comes Saturday, because the week goes round.

items.p: Today is Thursday. Two sleeps ago it was ____.
items.why: Hop back twice from Thursday: Wednesday, then Tuesday.

quiz.p: The Sun is going down and the sky is orange. Which part of the day is it?
quiz.why: It is evening. The Sun goes down in the evening. In the morning the Sun comes up.

quiz.p: A day has 4 parts. Morning and afternoon are over. Which part comes next?
quiz.why: Evening comes next. The order is morning, afternoon, evening, night. Picking night skips a part.

quiz.p: Put these in order, from first to last.
items: Put the peel in the bin
a: Put the peel in the bin
quiz.why: You must pick it before you can peel it, and peel it before you eat it. The peel goes in the bin last.

quiz.p: You are making lemon juice. What must you do first?
quiz.why: Cut the lemon first. You cannot squeeze, stir or drink before the lemon is open.

quiz.p: Look at the row. What comes just before 'eat breakfast'?
quiz.why: 'Brush teeth' is in the box just before 'eat breakfast'. 'Wash plate' comes after it.

quiz.p: Lunch comes after breakfast and before dinner.
quiz.why: True. The meals go breakfast, lunch, dinner. Lunch is in the middle, so it is after one and before the other.

quiz.p: Which day comes just after Thursday?
quiz.why: Friday comes just after Thursday. Wednesday comes before Thursday.

quiz.p: Which day comes just before Sunday?
quiz.why: Saturday comes just before Sunday. The week goes round, so Sunday follows Saturday. Monday comes after Sunday.

quiz.p: Look at the boxes. One week has ____ days.
quiz.why: There are 7 boxes. A week has seven days, from Sunday to Saturday.

quiz.p: Today is Tuesday. What day will tomorrow be?
quiz.why: Tomorrow is the day after today. After Tuesday comes Wednesday. Monday was yesterday.

quiz.p: Today is Monday. What day was yesterday?
quiz.why: Yesterday is the day before today. Before Monday comes Sunday.

quiz.p: Which of these did people choose?
quiz.why: People chose the name Wednesday. The Sun coming up and the sky getting dark happen without anyone choosing.

quiz.p: You can tell that it is Friday by looking at the Sun.
quiz.why: False. The Sun looks the same on every day. It can show you the part of the day, but not the name of the day.

A farmer waters the plants in the early morning or the evening, not in the hot afternoon.

A school or a class has a timetable: music on Tuesday, drawing on Friday.

open_questions.q: Why did people first choose seven days for a week?
open_questions.why_open: The seven-day week is thousands of years old. There are several ideas about where it came from. One is the Moon. Another is the seven lights people saw moving in the sky. No record settles it.
Everyone uses time. But scientists and thinkers still do not agree on what it is. They also ask why it only goes one way, from before to after.

open_questions.q: How does a bee remember what time of day she found food?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have known for about a hundred years that bees do this. How the bee's body joins a time to a place is still being studied.

open_questions.q: Does any other animal keep something like a week?
open_questions.why_open: Many living beings keep the time of day and the seasons. Nobody has clearly shown a wild animal counting days in sevens. It is hard to test.

maths.problem: You have lessons on 5 days of the week. The other days are rest days. How many rest days are there in a week?
maths.explain: A week has 7 days. Take away the 5 lesson days. Count on from 5 to 7: 6, 7. That is 2 days.

maths.problem: In Count the Claps, putting on chappals took 6 claps. Folding the towel took 14 claps. How many more claps did the towel take?

maths.context: In Count the Claps a grown-up clapped and counted while you did small jobs. This compares two of the counts.
maths.why_maths: The numbers tell you not just which job took longer, but how much longer.

maths.problem: The days go Sunday, Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, and then again. Today is Wednesday. What day is it 7 sleeps from now? Guess, then say why.
maths.explain: The days make a pattern of seven that repeats. Seven hops go once round the whole ring. So you land on the day you started from.
maths.context: On the Week Ring you hopped seven times and landed where you began. This asks you to say why.
maths.why_maths: Once you see that the week is a repeating pattern, you can tell the day far ahead without counting every sleep.

maths.problem: Kavya sorted her 8 day cards. Look at the picture. Which part of her day has the most cards? How many more cards does it have than the evening?

maths.why_maths: Sorting and counting shows you something about your day that you may not have noticed: mornings are full of small jobs.

roots.context: We put our day in order and went round the week. Now let us ask who made morning, and who made Monday.

deep_truth.truth: In the Window Test, the sky showed you that it was morning. It did not show you that it was Monday. The Sun makes morning and night. People made Monday. Long ago, people chose to count days in sevens and gave each day a name.
deep_truth.habit: We think Monday is just as real as morning. But morning comes from the Sun. Monday comes from people agreeing with each other.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Window Test you could tell the part of the day from the light. For the name of the day, you had to ask a person or look at a calendar. And people have used weeks of 8 days and 10 days.

three.who_am_i: Your body knows night and morning with no clock. You get sleepy when it is dark, and you wake when it is light.
three.what_is_life: Bees, roosters and tamarind trees keep the time of day too. None of them needs a name for the day.
three.what_is_this_world: The Earth keeps turning, so it is always morning somewhere. When you wake up in India, children in Mexico are going to bed.

roots.thread: The Earth turns round and round, and it does not stop. That one turning gives morning, afternoon, evening and night. People cut the turning into pieces and gave the pieces names, like Monday and week. The turning is one thing. The pieces and the names are ours.

teachings.teaching: This old Indian text says the Sun never really sets or rises. When people think the Sun is setting, it is making night here and day on the other side.
teachings.link: The Sun is always shining. Night comes to us when our side of the Earth turns away from the Sun.

teachings.teaching: Thiruvalluvar, the Tamil poet, says a crow can beat an owl in the daytime. So a king who wants to win must choose the right time.
teachings.link: The day belongs to the crow and the night to the owl. Each part of the day is the right time for someone.

teachings.teaching: This book of the Bible says that for everything there is a season, and a time for every purpose under heaven.
teachings.link: Your day has an order too. There is a time to wake, a time to eat, a time to play and a time to sleep.

science.text: In 1729 a French scientist, Jean-Jacques de Mairan, kept a plant in a dark cupboard. Most people think the plant was a touch-me-not. Their leaves still opened by day and folded at night. So living beings keep the time of day inside themselves.
Nobody is sure why people first chose seven days for a week. There are several ideas, and none is proved.

other_view.view: They say Monday is real too. The day we call Monday really comes, and the Sun really rises on it. Only the name is chosen. It is like naming a dog Raja. The dog is real, whatever name you give. Some of them also say seven was not just made up. The Moon takes about seven days to grow from a half Moon to a full Moon.

practice.title: One day in one minute
practice.say: Curl up small on the floor. This is night. Now breathe in slowly and stretch your arms up, like the Sun coming up. This is morning. Hold your arms high. This is afternoon. Breathe out and bring your arms down slowly. This is evening. Curl up again. This is night. Do it once more with your eyes closed. Could you feel where morning stopped and afternoon began?
practice.kid: Curl up small. This is night. Stretch up slowly. This is morning. Hold your arms high, then bring them down. Curl up again. Where did morning stop?

ask: Does a crow know it is Sunday? How could you find out?
