how_we_found_out.context: How did people find out why morning and night come? This card tells the true story of an Indian mathematician who said the Earth turns.
how_we_found_out.story: For a very long time, almost everyone thought the Earth stood still. They thought the Sun went round the Earth once a day, and that this made morning and night. It looks that way from your window. About 1,500 years ago an Indian mathematician, Aryabhata, said something different. He wrote a book called the Aryabhatiya. He says in it that he was 23 years old in the year 499. In this book he said that the Earth turns. He gave an example. A person in a moving boat sees the trees on the bank go backward. In the same way, he said, the stars only seem to move west. Most people then did not agree with him. They said the sky turned. In 1851 a French scientist, Léon Foucault, hung a heavy ball on a long wire in Paris and let it swing. Through the day, the line of the swing slowly turned over the floor. The floor was turning under the ball, because the Earth turns. Now anyone could see it.
how_we_found_out.who: Aryabhata, and much later Léon Foucault
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: The Earth stands still, and the Sun goes round it once a day. Aryabhata said the Earth turns. Foucault's swinging ball showed it.

science: Aryabhata, Aryabhatiya, Golapada 9 and 10 (the boat example and the turning Earth). Dated from the author's own statement that he was 23 in the year 3600 of the Kali Yuga, which is 499 CE.

Foucault, L. (1851). The pendulum shown at the Paris Observatory in February 1851 and then at the Panthéon. (American Physical Society, 'February 3, 1851: Léon Foucault demonstrates that Earth rotates'.)
Beling, I. (1929). Über das Zeitgedächtnis der Bienen. Zeitschrift für vergleichende Physiologie 9, 259-338.
Beer, K., Zupanc, G. K. H. and Helfrich-Förster, C. (2024). Ingeborg Beling and the time memory in honeybees: almost one hundred years of research. Journal of Comparative Physiology A.
Shimmura, T. and Yoshimura, T. (2013). Circadian clock determines the timing of rooster crowing. Current Biology 23(6), R231-R233.

de Mairan, J.-J. d'Ortous (1729). Observation botanique. Histoire de l'Académie Royale des Sciences, 35-36. (Reported by Marchant. The plant is usually taken to be Mimosa pudica, but this is not certain.)

The week: Encyclopaedia Britannica calls the week a unit with no astronomical basis. The Roman 8-day market week, the French Republican 10-day week (from 1793; sources differ on when it ended, so the unit gives no end date) and the sunset start of the Jewish and Islamic day were checked on the web. Zerubavel, E. (1985), The Seven Day Circle, is the standard book on the week. It was not opened for this lesson.
Aitareya Brahmana 3.44, in Martin Haug's translation (1863): the Sun never sets nor rises.

playtest: Walked through every flow as a family of two in a flat. The Day Cards Test needs one sheet of paper cut into 8, and works with the eight cards suggested in the parent note if the child has fewer than eight ideas. Of the swaps named there, two go wrong and two work, so the result is not known beforehand. The Window Test works at any time of day. The sky gives no clue to the day of the week, and any clue the child finds comes from people. Fill My Day was played in the head with 1, 2 and 4 players. Alone it takes about 8 turns. Round the Week takes about 6 rolls for 3 beans. The lemon juice robot does a pretend run first, so no food is wasted. Step minutes add up to each part's minutes. Facts looked up on the web while writing: Aryabhata's boat example (Gola 9) and the year 499, Foucault's pendulum in 1851, Beling's bees in 1929, the rooster study of 2013, de Mairan's plant in 1729, the Roman 8-day and French 10-day weeks, tamarind leaves folding at night, the four o'clock flower, hibiscus flowers lasting about a day, Thirukkural 481, Aitareya Brahmana 3.44, and the evening start of the Jewish and Islamic day. Two videos were confirmed by title and channel only, not watched. The third has no address yet. Not checked against a scholarly source: that the panchangam day starts at sunrise (several almanac sites say so), and the Tamil day names, which are in everyday use. The Chennai and Mexico City clock times were worked out from the two time zones.
